July 2025 – V1 Rev. 3 Table of Contents 1. Overview 2. HW System 3. Architecture 4. Host Interface 5. Compute 6. Software Suite 7. Networking 8. Putting It All Together 9. Performance Improvements 3 4 7 10 11 19 21 25 30 Introduction Deep Learning and Artificial Intelligence workloads continue to demand higher performance and lower power consumption. This technical paper introduces the next generation AI accelerator from Intel: the Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI accelerator. The new accelerator features the 5th generation of heterogenous AI acceleration architecture. The Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator was designed to provide state-of-the-art datacenter performance for all AI workloads, from generative applications such as large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models (image generation such as Stable Diffusion) to standard object recognition, classification, and voice dubbing.
The Intel® Gaudi® 2 AI accelerator, introduced in 2022, is supported by the Intel® Gaudi® software suite, which integrates the PyTorch framework. With the Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator we provide the next level of AI performance and power efficiency. Advancing from the Intel Gaudi 2 AI accelerator 7nm process, the Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator is manufactured in TSMC 5nm process, which provides improved area density and power efficiency.
Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator continues to push the boundaries of what is possible in performance and power efficiency. Built on the Intel Gaudi 2 AI accelerator architecture, Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator provides significant boosts in compute, memory bandwidth, and architectural efficiency.
The Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator features two compute dies, which together contain 8 MME engines, 64 TPC engines and 24x 200 Gbps RDMA NIC ports. In addition, the total of 8 HBM2e chips comprise a 128 GB unified High Bandwidth Memory (HBM).
The Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator excels at training and inference with 1.8 PFlops of FP8 and BF16 compute, 128 GB of HBM2e memory capacity, and 3.7 TB/s of HBM bandwidth.
As deep learning models continue to increase in size and complexity, the demand for efficient, high-performance matrix multiplication engines is set to rise. The MMEs in solutions like Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator are therefore of critical importance to the ongoing advancement of deep learning technologies.
The latest public model performance benchmarks are published at Model Performance for Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI Accelerators.
Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI Accelerator Technical Paper 2 Intel Gaudi 3 AI Accelerator Overview AI applications increasingly demand faster and more energy-efficient hardware solutions and the Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator was designed to answer the demand. With more than 2x FP8 GEMM FLOPs and more than 4x BF16 GEMM FLOPs compared to the Intel Gaudi 2 AI accelerator, Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator continues to provide state-of-the-art AI training performance. With 1.5x faster HBM bandwidth and 1.33x larger HBM capacity, the Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator provides an order-of-magnitude improvement in large language model inference performance compared to the Intel Gaudi 2 AI accelerator.
The Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator (Figure 1) features two identical compute dies, connected through a high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnect over an interposer bridge. The die-to-die connection is transparent to the software, providing performance and behavior equivalent to that of a large unified single die.
The Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator compute architecture is heterogeneous and includes two main compute engines – a Matrix Multiplication Engine (MME) and a fully programmable Tensor Processor Core (TPC) cluster. The MME is responsible for doing all operations that can be lowered to Matrix Multiplication, like fully connected layers, convolutions and batched-GEMMs. The TPC, a Very Long Instruction Word (VLIW) Single-Instruction Multiple-Data (SIMD) processor tailor-made for deep learning applications, is used to accelerate all non-GEMM operations.

* Create new deep learning models or migrate existing code in minutes.

This article shows how to run a typical inference use case on the Intel® Gaudi® AI accelerator. Learn how to select a model, set up the environment, run the workload, and then see a price-performance comparison. The accelerator supports PyTorch\* as the main framework for inference.

The following code guides you in how to:

* Get access to a node for Intel Gaudi AI accelerator on the Intel® Tiber™ Developer Cloud.
* Ensure that all the software is installed and configured properly by running the PyTorch version of the Docker\* image for the accelerator
* Select the model to run by loading the desired model repository and appropriate libraries for model acceleration.
* Run the model and extract the details for evaluation.

There are four methods for running inference on models:

1. Using Hugging Face\* models with the [Optimum Habana library](https://developer.habana.ai/get-started/hugging-face/)
2. Using built-in PyTorch models with the [Model References](https://developer.habana.ai/get-started/model-references/) [repository](https://developer.habana.ai/get-started/model-references/)
3. Automatically converting GPU-based models to be compatible with Intel Gaudi AI accelerators using the [GPU Migration](https://developer.habana.ai/get-started/gpu-migration-toolkit/) [toolkit](https://developer.habana.ai/get-started/gpu-migration-toolkit/)
4. Manually migrating PyTorch models in the public domain

The Optimum Habana library and the Model References repository contain fully optimized and fully documented model examples. Use them as a starting point for running a model.

This example shows model inference with Hugging Face by running the Meta\* Llama-2-70b model using the Optimum Habana library. Since Hugging Face models are used with an associated task, inference is run with the [text-generation](https://github.com/huggingface/optimum-habana/tree/main/examples/text-generation) [task](https://github.com/huggingface/optimum-habana/tree/main/examples/text-generation).

## Performance Evaluation

Before running the model, let's look at the performance measurements and a price-performance comparison to an equivalent H100 inference. In this case, the Llama-2-70b parameter model was selected using FP8, with 128 input tokens, 2048 output tokens, and four Intel Gaudi AI accelerators.1, 2

Figure 1. Performance cost differences

The tokens per dollar or inference runs per dollar are significantly higher than the NVIDIA\* solution.

 2 The model is compared to the same model configuration using the H100 GPU using NVIDIA published inference [benchmarks](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/performance/perf-overview.html) from June 25, 2024.

# IBM Cloud is First Service Provider to Deploy Intel Gaudi 3

IBM is the first cloud service provider to make Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI accelerators available to customers, a move designed to make powerful artificial intelligence capabilities more accessible and to directly address the high cost of specialized AI hardware.

For Intel, the rollout on IBM Cloud marks the first major commercial deployment of Gaudi 3, bringing choice to the market. By leveraging Intel Gaudi 3 on IBM Cloud, the two companies aim to help clients cost-effectively test, innovate and deploy GenAI solutions.

According to a [recent forecast](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-03-31-gartner-forecasts-worldwide-genai-spending-to-reach-644-billion-in-2025) by research firm Gartner, worldwide generative AI (GenAI) spending is expected to total $644 billion in 2025, an increase of 76.4% from 2024. The research found “GenAI will have a transformative impact across all aspects of IT spending markets, suggesting a future where AI technologies become increasingly integral to business operations and consumer products.”

For many enterprise customers, the benefits are clear when tools like GenAI automate tasks, improve workflows and drive innovation. But deploying AI applications demands significant computing power, often requiring expensive specialized processors that can keep many businesses from benefiting from AI.

Gaudi 3 AI accelerators are specifically designed to help meet the exploding demands for GenAI, large model inferencing and model fine-tuning while supporting an open development framework. Gaudi 3 is also ideal for multimodal large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

“By bringing Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators to IBM Cloud, we're enabling businesses to help scale generative AI workloads with optimized performance for inferencing and fine-tuning,” said Saurabh Kulkarni, vice president of Data Center AI Strategy at Intel. “This collaboration underscores our shared commitment to making AI more accessible and cost-effective for enterprises worldwide.”

## IBM Cloud is First Service Provider to Deploy Intel Gaudi 3

## How Enterprise Customers Use IBM Cloud

IBM Cloud serves a range of enterprise customers, particularly those in regulated industries, such as financial services, healthcare and life sciences, and the public sector.

Banks and insurance companies use the cloud for fraud detection or personalized customer service, while healthcare providers use it for accelerating drug discovery and development, AI-driven diagnostics, telemedicine platforms and real-time patient monitoring. Retailers use cloud technology for e-commerce platforms or inventory management. It’s also a go-to for companies looking to modernize old systems without giving up control or security.

Gaudi 3 is now available in the IBM Cloud regions of Frankfurt, Germany; Washington, D.C.; and Dallas, Texas.

Gaudi 3 is also being integrated into IBM’s broader AI infrastructure offerings. Customers can use Gaudi 3 via IBM Cloud Virtual Servers on the IBM Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) now. Customers will also be able to deploy across architectures starting in the second half of 2025. Support for Red Hat OpenShift and IBM’s watsonx AI platform is expected to be available this quarter.

“The ability to handle more data, and have higher performance, all of this is going to drive better adoption of AI for customers worldwide,” says Satinder Sethi, general manager of IBM Cloud Infrastructure Services. “Intel Gaudi 3 is giving customers more choice, more freedom and a more cost-effective platform of which AI hardware they want to use.”

IBM Cloud offers easily deployed hybrid cloud solutions, scalability, and affordability with Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI accelerators.

## At a glance:

* IBM Cloud is the first cloud services provider to make Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI accelerators available to its enterprise customers.1 Intel Gaudi 3 accelerators are designed for:
* Cost-effectiveness, security and resiliency.
* Flexibility with an open ecosystem.
* Hosting bigger models using fewer accelerators due to large memory.2

## Executive Summary

From the inception in 1981 of the first IBM personal PC, powered by the 8088 microprocessor, Intel and [IBM](https://www.ibm.com/cloud) have been helping customers and partners consistently achieve their goals. This long-term collaboration has driven innovation and delivered exceptional results across various technological eras. Today, [IBM and Intel](https://www.ibm.com/cloud/intel) are continuing that collaborative success by deploying [Intel® Gaudi® 3 AI accelerators](/content/www/us/en/products/details/processors/ai-accelerators/gaudi.html) as a service on IBM Cloud. This offering aims to help enterprises more cost-effectively scale AI and drive innovation while prioritizing openness, security, and resiliency. This collaboration will also enable support for Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators within [IBM’s watsonx AI](https://www.ibm.com/products/watsonx-ai) and data platform in Q2 2025.

## Challenge

There’s no doubt that AI can help drive enterprise efficiency and competitiveness. For example, generative AI (GenAI) can boost HR productivity by up to 8x,3 handle 97% of customer questions,4 and generate 60% of software development content.5

However, enterprises struggle to reach such tantalizing goals due to several cost and scalability concerns; the time and effort involved in choosing and deploying infrastructure that meets performance goals; and security, compliance/governance, and resilience requirements. These same challenges are compounded when enterprises consider deploying AI workloads in the hybrid cloud. Enterprises need trusted partners that can help them unlock the potential of GenAI.

## Solution

IBM and Intel have a long-standing collaborative relationship, and each have a vision of creating AI systems with total cost of ownership (TCO) advantages and enabling an open ecosystem to scale enterprise AI.

IBM Cloud is the first cloud service provider to make Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators available to its enterprise customers.1 IBM Cloud offerings include [Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators](http://www.ibm.com/cloud/gpu-ai-accelerator/intel-gaudi3) as part of its full-stack approach to GenAI.  Intel Gaudi 3 accelerators include AI-specific design and AI-centric features: These devices are specifically designed to help meet the exploding demands for GenAI, large model inferencing, and model fine-tuning while supporting an open development framework. In particular, Intel Gaudi 3 accelerators are ideal for multi-model large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which helps streamline the integration with IBM’s watsonx and data platform. Intel Core Ultra and 5th Gen Intel Xeon processors expand Intel’s unmatched AI portfolio, bringing AI to all.

## News

* December 14, 2023
* [Contact Intel PR](/content/www/us/en/newsroom/contact-public-relations-team.html)

NEW YORK, Dec. 14, 2023 – At its “AI Everywhere” launch in New York City today, Intel introduced an unmatched portfolio of AI products to enable customers’ AI solutions everywhere — across the data center, cloud, network, edge and PC.

Highlights include:

* The Intel® Core™ Ultra mobile processor family, the first built on the Intel 4 process technology and the first to benefit from the company’s largest architectural shift in 40 years, delivers Intel’s most power-efficient client processor and ushers in the age of the AI PC.
* The 5th Gen Intel® Xeon® processor family is built with AI acceleration in every core, bringing leaps in AI and overall performance and lowering total cost of ownership (TCO).
* Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger showed for the first time an Intel® Gaudi®3 AI accelerator, arriving on schedule next year.

“AI innovation is poised to raise the digital economy’s impact up to as much as one-third of global gross domestic product1,” Gelsinger said. “Intel is developing the technologies and solutions that empower customers to seamlessly integrate and effectively run AI in all their applications — in the cloud and, increasingly, locally at the PC and edge, where data is generated and used.”

Gelsinger showcased Intel’s expansive AI footprint, spanning cloud and enterprise servers to networks, volume clients and ubiquitous edge environments. He also reinforced that Intel is on track to deliver five new process technology nodes in four years.

“Intel is on a mission to bring AI everywhere through exceptionally engineered platforms, secure solutions and support for open ecosystems. Our AI portfolio gets even stronger with today’s launch of Intel Core Ultra ushering in the age of the AI PC and AI-accelerated 5th Gen Xeon for the enterprise,” Gelsinger said.

**Intel Core Ultra Powers AI PC and New Applications**

Intel Core Ultra represents the company’s largest architectural shift in 40 years and launches the AI PC generation with innovation on all fronts: CPU compute, graphics, power, battery life and profound new AI features. The AI PC represents the largest transformation of the PC experience in 20 years, since Intel® Centrino® untethered laptops to connect to Wi-Fi from anywhere.

Intel Core Ultra features Intel’s first client on-chip AI accelerator — the neural processing unit, or NPU — to enable a new level of power-efficient AI acceleration with 2.5x better power efficiency than the previous generation2. Its world-class GPU and leadership CPU are each also capable of speeding up AI solutions.

As important, Intel is partnering with more than 100 software vendors to bring several hundred AI-boosted applications to the PC market — a wide array of highly creative, productive and fun applications that will change the PC experience. For consumer and commercial customers, this means a larger and more extensive set of AI-enhanced applications will run great on Intel Core Ultra, particularly compared to competing platforms. For example, content creators working in Adobe Premiere Pro will enjoy 40% better performance versus the competition3.

Google.overview: Google offers a family of custom AI accelerators called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) through its Google Cloud platform. Multiple TPU generations are available, ranging from early v2/v3 models to the latest v8 variants designed for both training and inference workloads. The TPUs are offered as on‑demand accelerator resources with various pricing and discount options, and they are used by enterprise customers and AI developers for large‑scale model training and inference. Google provides detailed performance specifications, including TFLOPs, high‑bandwidth memory, and interconnect bandwidth, for each generation.

requirements.requirement: Which generations of Google Tensor Processing Units (TPU) are currently available to cloud customers?

findings.finding: Google Cloud currently provides several TPU generations to customers: the second‑ and third‑generation TPUs (v2 and v3, GA), the fifth‑generation TPUs (v5e and v5p), the sixth‑generation TPU (v6e, also called Trillium), the seventh‑generation TPU (v7x, Ironwood), and the newly announced eighth‑generation TPUs (TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference).
Google Cloud currently offers multiple TPU generations to customers, including TPU v2, v3, v4, v5e, v7x, 8t, and 8i.

Google Cloud currently offers three generations of Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) for customers: the fourth‑generation Cloud TPU v4, the fifth‑generation Cloud TPU v5e (generally available), and the newly announced fifth‑generation Cloud TPU v5p. All three are provisioned through Google Cloud as on‑demand accelerator resources. These generations represent the TPU models that can be selected by cloud customers for AI training and inference workloads.

requirements.summary: Google Cloud provides several TPU generations to customers: the second‑ and third‑generation TPUs (v2 and v3), the fourth‑generation v4, the fifth‑generation v5e and v5p, the sixth‑generation v6e (Trillium), the seventh‑generation v7x (Ironwood), and the newly announced eighth‑generation TPUs (TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference).

requirements.requirement: What performance metrics (TFLOPs, memory, interconnect) are specified for each available TPU generation?

findings.finding: A Cloud TPU v4 chip provides 275 TFLOPs peak compute (bf16 or int8), 32 GiB HBM2 memory with 1200 GB/s bandwidth, and a 3D‑mesh interconnect; a full v4 pod of 4096 chips delivers 1.1 exaflops peak compute and 1.1 PB/s all‑reduce bandwidth.

Performance metrics for the available TPU generations are disclosed by Google. Cloud TPU v5e achieves a 2.3× price‑performance improvement over the previous‑generation TPU v4 according to MLPerf™ 3.1 training results. Cloud TPU v5p delivers more than 2× greater FLOPS and 3× larger high‑bandwidth memory (HBM) than TPU v4, and each v5p chip connects via a 4,800 Gbps inter‑chip interconnect in a 3‑D torus topology. A TPU v5p pod is composed of 8,960 chips, providing massive scale for large‑model training.

requirements.summary: A Cloud TPU v4 chip delivers 275 TFLOPs peak compute, 32 GiB HBM2 memory with 1.2 TB/s bandwidth, and a 3‑D mesh interconnect; the v5e generation provides a 2.3× price‑performance improvement over v4; the v5p generation offers more than double the FLOPS, three times the high‑bandwidth memory, and a 4.8 Tbps inter‑chip interconnect in a 3‑D torus topology.

requirements.requirement: What is the pricing structure for Google Cloud TPU usage (per‑hour rates, discounts, committed‑use pricing)?

findings.finding: Google Cloud TPU pricing is expressed per chip‑hour and varies by generation and commitment level. On‑demand rates include $4.20 per chip‑hour for a v5p chip, $1.20 for a v5e chip, and $3.22 for a v4 pod chip. Flex‑Start pricing offers roughly 50 % discount (e.g., $2.10 per hour for v5p). One‑year committed use reduces prices to $2.94 (v5p) and $0.84 (v5e) per hour, while three‑year commitments lower them further to $1.89 and $0.54 respectively. Regional variations are listed (e.g., South Carolina rates).

Google Cloud TPU pricing is usage‑based: e.g., TPU V2 single (8 cores) costs $5.40 per hour on‑demand, and a TPU V3 pod (32 cores) costs $36.80 per hour. Discounted rates are available via the Gemini Enterprise Flexible Savings Plan (1‑year reduces the V2 single to $4.86/h, 3‑year to $4.32/h) and through committed‑use reservations that lower prices for long‑term contracts.

requirements.summary: Google Cloud TPU pricing is expressed per chip‑hour and varies by generation: on‑demand rates include $4.20 per hour for a v5p chip, $1.20 for a v5e chip, $3.22 for a v4 pod chip, $5.40 for a v2 single chip, and $36.80 for a v3 pod. Discount programs such as Flex‑Start (≈50 % off) and 1‑year or 3‑year committed‑use contracts further reduce rates (e.g., v5p $2.94/yr, $1.89/3‑yr; v5e $0.84/yr, $0.54/3‑yr).

requirements.requirement: Which enterprise cloud customers or AI developers are known to run production workloads on Google Cloud TPUs?

findings.finding: Enterprise customers running production workloads on Google Cloud TPUs include EssentialAI (using TPU v5p for model training), Anthropic (multi‑billion‑dollar agreement for TPU 7x and 8th‑generation platforms), and LG CNS (using Cloud TPUs for defect detection in LCD panel production).

requirements.summary: Enterprise customers running production workloads on Google Cloud TPUs include EssentialAI (using v5p for model training), Anthropic (with a multi‑billion‑dollar agreement for v7x and eighth‑generation platforms), and LG CNS (leveraging TPUs for defect detection in LCD panel production).

AMD.overview: AMD’s AI computing offering centers on the Instinct line of accelerators, which includes the MI100, MI300 series, MI325X, MI350 series, and the newer MI355X GPUs. These devices feature high‑bandwidth HBM3e memory (up to 288 GB) and deliver AI performance ranging from teraflops to tens of petaflops, with support for FP8, FP16 and sparsity optimizations. AMD’s accelerators are available through major cloud providers such as AWS, Oracle Cloud, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure, and are used by enterprise AI developers and partners like Meta, Cohere and AT&T. Recent product announcements introduced the MI350 series, Helion and Helios rack‑scale platforms, and a roadmap that targets the MI500 series and large‑scale deployments through 2027.

requirements.requirement: What AI‑focused GPU or accelerator product lines does AMD currently sell (e.g., Instinct MI series)?

findings.finding: AMD offers AI‑focused accelerator product lines under the Instinct brand, including the Instinct MI300 series, the MI325X accelerator, and the MI350 series GPUs.

AMD offers the Instinct family of AI accelerators. The product line includes the Instinct MI100 accelerator announced in 2020, the newer Instinct MI300 series (MI300, MI300X) and the Instinct MI355X GPUs highlighted on AMD’s AI infrastructure page. These GPUs are positioned for high‑performance computing and AI workloads.

requirements.summary: AMD’s AI‑focused accelerator portfolio is marketed under the Instinct brand. The line includes the Instinct MI100 accelerator, the MI300 series (MI300, MI300X), the MI325X accelerator, the MI350 series (including MI350P), and the newer MI355X GPUs, all positioned for high‑performance computing and AI workloads.

requirements.requirement: What are the key technical specifications of the latest AMD Instinct MI accelerator (compute performance, memory, bandwidth)?

findings.finding: The Instinct MI325X accelerator provides 256 GB of HBM3e memory with 6 TB/s on‑package bandwidth and delivers up to 1.3 PFLOPs FP16 performance (2.61 PFLOPs with sparsity) and up to 5.22 PFLOPs FP8 performance with structured sparsity. The newer Instinct MI350 series expands memory to 288 GB HBM3e, bandwidth to 8 TB/s, and supports similar high‑throughput FP8 and FP16 compute.

The AMD Instinct MI355X accelerator, launched in June 2025, provides 2.3 TB of HBM3E memory, 8.0 TB/s per OAM memory bandwidth, and AI performance up to 80.5 PFLOPs (MXFP4) and 1,258.4 TFLOPs FP16, representing the latest announced specifications for an AMD Instinct GPU.

The Instinct MI100 accelerator delivers more than 10 teraflops of double‑precision (FP64) performance, making it the first HPC GPU to break the 10 TFLOP FP64 barrier. It is built on AMD’s CDNA architecture and is intended to be paired with 2nd‑generation EPYC CPUs. The press release does not disclose memory capacity or memory bandwidth for the MI100.

requirements.summary: The Instinct MI325X accelerator provides 256 GB of HBM3e memory with 6 TB/s on‑package bandwidth and delivers up to 1.3 PFLOPs FP16 performance (2.61 PFLOPs with sparsity) and up to 5.22 PFLOPs FP8. The MI350 series expands memory to 288 GB HBM3e and bandwidth to 8 TB/s while offering comparable high‑throughput FP8 and FP16 compute. The MI355X, announced in 2025, is reported to have 2.3 TB of HBM3E memory, 8 TB/s bandwidth, and AI performance up to 80.5 PFLOPs (MXFP4) and 1,258.4 TFLOPs FP16. The earlier MI100 delivers more than 10 TFLOPs double‑precision performance.

requirements.requirement: What official list or typical contract pricing is publicly disclosed for AMD Instinct AI accelerators?

findings.finding: AMD disclosed an internal estimate for a server built around a single Instinct MI350P GPU at $327,238.40 USD; the comparable NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 server public list price was $265,928.24 USD, providing the only publicly referenced pricing figure for an AMD Instinct accelerator.

requirements.summary: AMD disclosed an internal estimate for a server built around a single Instinct MI350P GPU priced at $327,238.40 USD, providing the only publicly referenced pricing figure for an AMD Instinct accelerator.

requirements.requirement: Which cloud service providers or AI developers have integrated AMD Instinct GPUs into their production offerings?

findings.finding: AWS, Oracle Cloud, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure list AMD Instinct GPUs in their AI compute catalogs, and Meta has integrated custom Instinct GPUs into its super‑intelligence infrastructure.

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) is the first hyperscaler to deploy AMD Instinct GPUs in production, offering MI355X (2025) and MI300X (2024) in its OCI Supercluster instances. Enterprise AI developers such as Cohere and Fireworks AI run training and inference workloads on these OCI‑based AMD accelerators.

AMD’s Instinct GPUs are integrated into several cloud and enterprise offerings. Microsoft Azure collaborates with AMD for HPC instances featuring Instinct accelerators. AT&T uses Instinct MI355X GPUs for telecom AI training, while Maincode, 310 AI, and MindWalk run Instinct MI300X/MI300 series GPUs on the Vultr cloud platform. Oracle has announced a plan to deploy 50,000 Instinct GPUs beginning in 2026.

requirements.summary: AWS, Oracle Cloud, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure list AMD Instinct GPUs in their AI compute catalogs, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure was the first hyperscaler to deploy MI300X and MI355X accelerators in production Supercluster instances. Enterprise AI developers such as Cohere, Fireworks AI, 310 AI, Maincode, MindWalk and AT&T also run workloads on Instinct GPUs, and Meta has integrated custom Instinct GPUs into its internal AI infrastructure.

requirements.requirement: What new AMD AI accelerator products or major roadmap updates have been announced in the past year?

findings.finding: In the past year AMD announced the Instinct MI350 series of AI accelerators (2026), launched the Helion rack‑scale Agentic AI compute platform at the OCP 2026 keynote, and expanded its partnership with Meta to deliver custom Instinct GPUs for a multi‑gigawatt deployment.

In the past year AMD announced several AI accelerator updates: the MI350P GPU (July 2026) as part of the MI400 series, the Helios rack‑scale platform built on MI455X GPUs, the upcoming MI500 series slated for 2027, and the MI355X GPU (October 2025) now available in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

In the past year AMD announced the Helios AI Rackscale solution, an exaflop‑class platform designed for frontier inference, training, and fine‑tuning at massive scale. The company also disclosed commitments of up to 6 GW of AI infrastructure with partners such as OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle, and a planned deployment of 50,000 Instinct GPUs in 2026, indicating a significant roadmap expansion for AI accelerators.

requirements.summary: In the past year AMD announced the Instinct MI350 series (including the MI350P GPU) and launched the Helion rack‑scale Agentic AI compute platform, while also unveiling the Helios platform built on MI455X GPUs and previewing the MI500 series for 2027. The company expanded its partnership with Meta for custom GPUs, committed up to 6 GW of AI infrastructure with partners such as OpenAI and Microsoft, and plans to deploy 50,000 Instinct GPUs in 2026.

caveats: Pricing information is limited to a single internal server estimate; no official list prices for individual GPUs are disclosed.
Technical specifications are provided for select models (MI325X, MI350, MI355X, MI100); detailed specs for other Instinct GPUs are not covered.
Cloud customer references are based on announcements and may not reflect the full set of production deployments.
Roadmap details (e.g., MI500 series, Helios platform) are announced but not confirmed as generally available, so availability status is uncertain.

Intel Corp.overview: Intel Corp provides a portfolio of AI accelerator hardware that includes the Intel® Gaudi family (first‑generation Gaudi, Gaudi 2, and Gaudi 3) and the Intel® Data Center GPU Flex/Max series based on the Xe‑HPC architecture. The Gaudi line targets data‑center training and inference, while Xe‑HPC GPUs address high‑performance compute and graphics workloads. Intel also embeds AI acceleration in its 5th Gen Xeon processors, offering on‑chip matrix and vector engines for heterogeneous AI workloads. These products are positioned for cloud service providers, OEMs, and enterprise AI developers in both the United States and Europe.

requirements.requirement: What AI accelerator products does Intel currently offer (e.g., Habana Gaudi, Xe‑HPC GPUs)?

findings.finding: Intel offers a portfolio of AI accelerator products that includes the Intel® Gaudi family (first‑generation Gaudi, Gaudi 2, and Gaudi 3) and the Intel® Data Center GPU Flex Series, which are positioned for data‑center training and inference workloads.

Intel currently offers AI accelerator products that include the Intel Gaudi series (Gaudi 2 and the newly announced Gaudi 3) and the Intel Xe‑HPC GPUs sold under the Data Center GPU Max series (e.g., Max 1550). The Xe GPU architecture also spans Xe‑LP, Xe‑HPG and Xe‑HP variants for integrated, discrete and data‑center use cases.

Intel’s AI accelerator portfolio includes the Gaudi family, with the next‑generation Intel® Gaudi®3 AI accelerator announced for release in 2024, and AI‑enabled processors such as the 5th Gen Intel® Xeon® family that embed AI acceleration in each core.

requirements.summary: Intel offers a portfolio of AI accelerator products that includes the Intel® Gaudi family (first‑generation Gaudi, Gaudi 2, and Gaudi 3) and the Intel® Data Center GPU Flex Series (Xe‑HPC GPUs sold under the Data Center GPU Max line). The Xe architecture also spans Xe‑LP, Xe‑HPG and Xe‑HP variants for integrated, discrete and data‑center use cases, and AI‑enabled processors such as the 5th Gen Intel® Xeon family embed AI acceleration in each core.

requirements.requirement: What are the technical specifications of the latest Intel AI accelerator (e.g., Habana Gaudi 2 or Xe‑HPC) regarding compute performance and memory?

findings.finding: The latest Intel AI accelerator, the Intel® Gaudi 3, delivers up to 1,678 TFLOPS of FP8 and BF16 matrix‑multiply performance, 28.7 TFLOPS of BF16 vector compute, 128 GB of HBM memory with 3.7 TB/s bandwidth, 96 MB on‑die SRAM, 1,200 GB/s bidirectional networking, and a PCIe Gen5 x16 host interface providing 128 GB/s peak bandwidth.

The Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator delivers 4× AI compute for BF16 and 1.5× the memory bandwidth of its Gaudi 2 predecessor. It contains 64 Tensor Processor Cores and eight Matrix Multiplication Engines, and provides up to 20% higher inference throughput and roughly 2× price‑performance versus Nvidia H100 on LLaMa 2 70B1 workloads.

The Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (Xe‑HPC) features 128 Xe‑cores, 128 ray‑tracing units, 1,024 Xe Matrix Extensions engines, 1,024 vector engines, a 600 W TDP, and 128 GB of HBM2e memory delivering 3,276.8 GB/s bandwidth.

requirements.summary: The latest Intel AI accelerator, Gaudi 3, delivers up to 1,678 TFLOPS of FP8/BF16 matrix‑multiply performance, 28.7 TFLOPS of BF16 vector compute, 128 GB of HBM memory with 3.7 TB/s bandwidth, 96 MB on‑die SRAM, and 1,200 GB/s bidirectional networking via a PCIe Gen5 x16 interface. It provides 4× AI compute for BF16 compared with Gaudi 2 and roughly 2× price‑performance versus Nvidia H100 on LLaMa 2 70B1 workloads, featuring 64 Tensor Processor Cores and eight Matrix Multiplication Engines. The Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (Xe‑HPC) includes 128 Xe‑cores, 128 ray‑tracing units, 1,024 Xe Matrix Extensions, 1,024 vector engines, a 600 W TDP, and 128 GB of HBM2e delivering 3,276.8 GB/s bandwidth.

IBM Cloud is the first cloud service provider to deploy Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerators in production, offering the hardware in its Frankfurt (Germany), Washington, D.C., and Dallas (Texas) regions and integrating it with IBM’s watsonx AI platform and Virtual Private Cloud services.
